prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

U0101: MFCR currently identifies these flights by highlighting them in red, as shown in Figure 3 (see close to KCLT at the top right of the large pane), and it provides the TMC with the means to identify estimated time savings for each flight if it were to be rerouted once within the Center’s airspace.
U0102: In some cases, waiting for MFCR to add more flights in the reroute group will increase total flight-time savings and avoid the need to coordinate multiple groups.
U0103: TMCs can use this information in combination with the estimate in the savings-decay graph to decide when to start coordinating the reroute recommendation.
U0104: Figure 4: Reroute Savings Decay Over Time 4.3 CONVECTIVE WEATHER MODEL MFCR uses outputs from FAA’s Corridor Integrated Weather System (CIWS) and Convective Weather Avoidance Model (CWAM) to identify routes that will avoid convective cells.
U0105: CIWS forecasts the growth, decay, and movement of convective weather (see Figure 5).
U0106: Forecasts are updated every five minutes with a two-hour look-ahead time in five-minute increments.
U0107: This allows MFCR to identify alternative routes that remain clear of predicted weather between the MSP and RCF.
U0108: Figure 5: CIWS and CWAM Forecast Sample CWAM provides polygons, from FL250 to FL450 in 1,000 foot increments, around convective cells that pilots are predicted to deviate around, based on storm intensity, echo tops, and look-ahead time.
U0109: A CWAM polygon is identified by the percentage of pilots who would deviate around the storm at that distance based on extensive historical data.
U0110: For example, a 70% CWAM polygon represents a region that 70% of pilots would avoid.
U0111: A 70% CWAM polygon will be smaller (or sometimes the same), with boundaries closer to the weather cells, than a 60% CWAM polygon.
U0112: Figure 6: CIWS Cell and Corresponding 60, 70, & 80% CWAM Polygons Figure 6 shows an example of the difference between 60%, 70%, and 80% CWAM polygons.
U0113: CWAM polygons are updated with the CIWS forecast.
U0114: MFCR currently uses 70% CWAM polygons for weather avoidance when generating reroute recommendations, but it can be adapted to use polygon-based convective weather model outputs from other sources, if desired.
U0115: MFCR logic includes gap detection and rejection logic to ensure that a gap between CWAM polygons is large enough to safely route aircraft.
U0116: This function includes a distance buffer that will reject a route amendment if it will go through a gap that is narrower than 50 nautical miles laterally on either side of the route to the predicted cells at the time the aircraft reaches the point closest to the cells (see Figure 7).
U0117: The gap-width parameter is user adjustable.
U0118: If convective cells are predicted to encroach on one side of a trajectory but not on the other (blue polygons in left graphic in Figure 7), it is generally not considered an operational problem because there is room for flight crews to maneuver around the cell.
U0119: MFCR avoids narrow gaps, which are defined as a condition where cells are predicted to be on both sides of the trajectory at points within 50 nautical miles along-track distance of one another (pair of yellow polygons in right graphic of Figure 7).
U0120: Figure 7: MFCR Gap Detection 50 nm 4.4 MFCR USE CASE The table below summarizes the process to implement a reroute using MFCR.
U0121: Step 1: Traffic Management Coordinator (TMC) Evaluation, Approval, and Dissemination • The MFCR display and interface resides in the TMU and continually runs in the background.
U0122: The adjustable parameters (e.g., savings threshold, convective cell buffers) are set by the user. • When MFCR identifies reroutes that could save more time than the minimum savings threshold, it posts a list of each flight grouping and a list of those flights in order of greatest flight time savings.
U0123: Each new MFCR group posted to the list triggers an audible alert. • The traffic managers on duty hear the alert and review and modify the proposed MFCR route(s) as needed.
